concept_name: Diagonals and medians split area equally

item.question: The diagonals of an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle meet at O. Find the area of each of the four triangles.
steps: The rectangle has area 8 × 6 = 48 cm².
Adjacent triangles have equal halves of a diagonal as bases and the same height, so equal areas.
All four are equal: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².
item.answer: Each triangle is 12 cm², even though they are not congruent
item.text:
Worked example: The diagonals of an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle meet at O. Find the area of each of the four triangles.
1. The rectangle has area 8 × 6 = 48 cm².
2. Adjacent triangles have equal halves of a diagonal as bases and the same height, so equal areas.
3. All four are equal: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².
Answer: Each triangle is 12 cm², even though they are not congruent

item.question: BC = 6 cm and line l is parallel to BC, 4 cm away. Find the area of a triangle on BC with its top on l, and say how it changes as the top moves.
steps: Base = 6 cm, height = 4 cm for every position of the top.
Moving the top changes the slanting sides, not the height.
item.answer: Always 12 cm²: equal areas; only the perimeter changes
item.text:
Worked example: BC = 6 cm and line l is parallel to BC, 4 cm away. Find the area of a triangle on BC with its top on l, and say how it changes as the top moves.
1. Base = 6 cm, height = 4 cm for every position of the top.
2. Area = 1/2 × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².
3. Moving the top changes the slanting sides, not the height.
Answer: Always 12 cm²: equal areas; only the perimeter changes

item.question: B and C are 3 cm below line l and BC = 8 cm. Find the smallest possible value of AB + AC with A on l.
steps: Reflect C in l: C′ is 3 cm above l, so 6 cm above the line BC, directly over C.
BC′ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 6: √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10.
The straight line BC′ crosses l halfway across, above the midpoint of BC.
item.answer: The smallest AB + AC is 10 cm, with A on the perpendicular bisector of BC

2. BC′ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 6: √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10.
3. The straight line BC′ crosses l halfway across, above the midpoint of BC.
Answer: The smallest AB + AC is 10 cm, with A on the perpendicular bisector of BC

video.title: What are the blue region and the square?
video.description: Three identical squares are placed in an L shape, with a red triangle and a blue triangle on them. The red triangle equals one whole square, the blue triangle is a quarter of a square, and these give the blue area and the area of each square.
video.anchor: the book's three identical squares ABCD, BCEF and BFGH with the red triangle DCH and the blue triangle left of the line DH
maths_rules: squares ABCD and BCEF sit side by side and BFGH sits on top of BCEF, so H is directly above B, a side length s above B
red triangle DCH: base DC = s and height CH = CB + BH = 2s, so area = 1/2 × s × 2s = s², one whole square
the line DH climbs 2s for a run of s, so it climbs s (the height of ABCD) after a run of s/2, and meets AB at its midpoint
blue triangle: legs s and s/2, area = 1/2 × s × s/2 = s²/4, one quarter of a square
(i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units
(ii) blue + red = s² + s²/4 = 5s²/4 = 180, so s²/4 = 36 and s² = 144 sq. units (side 12)

final_answer.spoken: the blue region is twelve point two five square units, and each square is one hundred forty four square units

item.question: ABCD, BCEF and BFGH are identical squares, with H directly above B. The red region is the triangle DCH and the blue region is the part of square ABCD to the left of the line DH. (i) If the area of the red region is 49 sq. units, what is the area of the blue region? (ii) In another version, if the blue and red regions together are 180 sq. units, what is the area of each square?
steps: Let each square have side s. Red: base DC = s, height CH = 2s, so area 1/2 × s × 2s, which is s².
DH rises 2s over a run of s, so it crosses AB at its midpoint: the blue triangle has legs s and s/2, area one quarter of s².
(i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units.
(ii) Blue + red is five quarters of s², so s² = 180 × 4 ÷ 5 = 144 sq. units.
item.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 6): ABCD, BCEF and BFGH are identical squares, with H directly above B. The red region is the triangle DCH and the blue region is the part of square ABCD to the left of the line DH. (i) If the area of the red region is 49 sq. units, what is the area of the blue region? (ii) In another version, if the blue and red regions together are 180 sq. units, what is the area of each square?
1. Let each square have side s. Red: base DC = s, height CH = 2s, so area 1/2 × s × 2s, which is s².
2. DH rises 2s over a run of s, so it crosses AB at its midpoint: the blue triangle has legs s and s/2, area one quarter of s².
3. (i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units.
4. (ii) Blue + red is five quarters of s², so s² = 180 × 4 ÷ 5 = 144 sq. units.
Answer: (i) 12.25 sq. units (ii) 144 sq. units

item.text:

video.title: Which path to the river is shortest?
video.description: A water carrier walks from a house to a river bank and then to a water tank. The video treats the river bank as a mirror, reflects the tank, and joins the house to the reflection with a straight line. Where that line meets the bank is the best place to fill water.
video.anchor: the book's map: a house, a river bank above it and a water tank, with the water carrier's walk from the house to the bank and on to the tank
maths_rules: the river bank is a line l; the house H and the tank T are on the same side of it
reflect T in l to get T'; for every point P on l, PT = PT'
so HP + PT = HP + PT', which is the length of a path from H to T' that bends at P
the shortest path from H to T' is the straight line HT', so the best P is where HT' meets l
any other P on l gives a bent path H to P to T', which is longer than the straight line HT'
the walk is H to P to T, as long as the straight line HT'

final_answer.value: Reflect the tank in the river bank; the straight line from the house to the reflection meets the bank at the best point
final_answer.spoken: the best spot is where the straight line meets the river bank

item.question: Gopal needs to carry water from the river to his water tank. He starts from his house. What is the shortest path from his house to the river and then to the water tank? Recreate the map and trace it.
steps: Treat the river bank as a mirror line and reflect the water tank to the far side of it.
Join the house to the reflected tank with a straight line.
Where this line meets the river bank is the best point to fill water.
Walk house to that point, then to the real tank: this is as long as the straight line, the shortest possible.
item.answer: Reflect the tank in the river bank; the straight line from the house to the reflection meets the bank at the best point

item.question: Find the area of the quadrilateral ABCD given that AC = 22 cm, BM = 3 cm, DN = 3 cm, BM is perpendicular to AC, and DN is perpendicular to AC.
steps_tex: The diagonal $AC$ splits $ABCD$ into $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ACD$.
Area of $\triangle ABC = \frac{1}{2} \times 22 \times 3 = 33\text{ cm}^2$. Area of $\triangle ACD = \frac{1}{2} \times 22 \times 3 = 33\text{ cm}^2$.
steps: The diagonal AC splits ABCD into ΔABC and ΔACD.
Area of ΔABC = 1/2 × 22 × 3 = 33 cm². Area of ΔACD = 1/2 × 22 × 3 = 33 cm².
Area of ABCD = 33 + 33 = 66 cm².
item.text:
$1$. The diagonal $AC$ splits $ABCD$ into $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ACD$.
$2$. Area of $\triangle ABC = \frac{1}{2} \times 22 \times 3 = 33\text{ cm}^2$. Area of $\triangle ACD = \frac{1}{2} \times 22 \times 3 = 33\text{ cm}^2$.
$3$. Area of $ABCD = 33 + 33 = 66\text{ cm}^2$.
Answer: $66\text{ cm}^2$

maths_rules: let the rectangle have length L and width W; each blue triangle has a full side of length L as its base

rectangle = L × W, so blue is 1/2 of the rectangle wherever the tips meet

item.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 4): What fraction of the total area of the rectangle is the area of the blue region? (Two blue triangles stand on the top and bottom sides of the rectangle, with their tips meeting at a point inside.)
1. Each blue triangle has a full side of the rectangle as base: the length L.
2. Their heights, from the shared point to the top and to the bottom, add up to the width W.
3. Blue = 1/2 × L × h1 + 1/2 × L × h2 = 1/2 × L × (h1 + h2) = 1/2 × L × W.
Answer: Half of the rectangle is blue

likewise triangle CQR = 1/4 of triangle CBD; so APS + CQR = 1/4 (ABD + CBD) = 1/4 of ABCD

four corners = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 of ABCD; inner PQRS = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2 of ABCD

lp_text.concept_name: Practice: polygon areas by splitting and subtracting

item.question: Give a method to obtain a quadrilateral whose area is half that of a given quadrilateral.
steps: Mark the midpoints of the four sides and join them in order.
Each corner triangle cut off is one quarter of the triangle made by a diagonal (both sides are halved).
The four corners together are one quarter of each pair of diagonal triangles, so half the quadrilateral; the inner quadrilateral is the other half.
item.answer: Join the midpoints of the sides in order; the inner quadrilateral has half the area
item.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 5): Give a method to obtain a quadrilateral whose area is half that of a given quadrilateral.
1. Mark the midpoints of the four sides and join them in order.
2. Each corner triangle cut off is one quarter of the triangle made by a diagonal (both sides are halved).
3. The four corners together are one quarter of each pair of diagonal triangles, so half the quadrilateral; the inner quadrilateral is the other half.
Answer: Join the midpoints of the sides in order; the inner quadrilateral has half the area

concept_name: Turn a parallelogram into a rectangle

item.question: A parallelogram has base 9 cm and height 5 cm. Cut and slide it into a rectangle and find its area.
steps: Cut along a height of 5 cm and slide the triangle across.
The rectangle is 9 cm long and 5 cm high.
Area = 9 × 5 = 45 cm².
item.answer: 45 cm², the same as the parallelogram

concept_name: Base times height, with any base

item.question: A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 6 cm. The height on the 10 cm side is 4.8 cm. Find the area and the height on the 6 cm side.
steps: With base 6 cm: 6 × height = 48.
Height = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm.
item.answer: Area 48 cm²; the height on the 6 cm side is 8 cm
item.text:
Worked example: A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 6 cm. The height on the 10 cm side is 4.8 cm. Find the area and the height on the 6 cm side.

3. Height = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm.

item.question: Observe the parallelograms (a) to (g) drawn on a grid, all on equal bases between the same two grid lines. (i) What can we say about the areas of all these parallelograms? (ii) What can we say about their perimeters? Which figure appears to have the maximum perimeter, and which has the minimum perimeter?
steps_tex: (i): Each has the same base and the same height, so each has the same area, base $\times$ height.
(ii): The perimeter is twice the base plus twice the slanting side.
The more a parallelogram leans, the longer its slanting sides, so the larger its perimeter.
item.answer_tex: (i): All have equal areas. (ii): The perimeters differ: $(g)$, leaning most, appears largest and $(a)$, almost upright, smallest
